stem: What is crop rotation?

options.content: Growing different crops in turn on the same land in a planned sequence
options.rationale: Correct.

options.content: Growing the same crop on the same land every year
options.rationale: That is monoculture.

options.content: Growing two or more crops mixed together in the same field at once
options.rationale: That is intercropping (mixed cropping).

options.content: Moving to new land each time the soil becomes infertile
options.rationale: That is shifting cultivation.

explanation: Rotation changes the crop on each field in a repeated, planned order.

stem: Why should a legume be grown before maize in a rotation?

options.content: Legume residues release fixed nitrogen for the maize
options.rationale: Correct: maize is a heavy feeder of nitrogen.

options.content: Legumes remove all the weeds from the soil
options.rationale: Legumes do not remove all weeds.

options.content: Maize cannot grow at all unless a legume is planted first
options.rationale: Maize can grow, but needs more fertiliser.

options.content: Legumes make the soil more acid for maize
options.rationale: This is not a reason for the order.

explanation: Nitrogen fixed by *Rhizobium* in legume nodules benefits the following heavy feeder.

stem: Why do crops of different families follow one another in a rotation?

options.content: Different families need no fertiliser at all
options.rationale: All crops need nutrients.

options.content: Crops of the same family cannot be sold together at the market
options.rationale: Marketing is not the reason.

options.content: Pests and diseases of one family find no host and die out
options.rationale: Correct: many attack only one family.

options.content: Different families all have the same root depth
options.rationale: Root depths differ; that is another principle.

explanation: Changing family breaks pest, disease and parasitic-weed cycles.

stem: Which sequence breaks the life cycle of witchweed best?

options.content: Maize, then sorghum, then pearl millet
options.rationale: All three are hosts of witchweed.

options.content: Maize, then maize, then maize
options.rationale: Continuous maize builds up witchweed.

options.content: Maize, then groundnuts, then cotton
options.rationale: Correct: groundnuts and cotton are non-hosts.

options.content: Sorghum, then maize, then sorghum
options.rationale: Cereal hosts keep witchweed going.

explanation: Witchweed parasitises cereals; non-host crops reduce the seed bank.

stem: Why are deep-rooted and shallow-rooted crops alternated?

options.content: Deep-rooted crops add nitrogen to the subsoil from the air
options.rationale: Only legumes fix nitrogen, whatever their roots.

options.content: Shallow-rooted crops need no water at all
options.rationale: All crops need water.

options.content: Root depth decides the market price of the crop
options.rationale: Price is not linked to root depth.

options.content: Nutrients and water are drawn from different soil layers
options.rationale: Correct: the whole profile is used and structure improves.

explanation: Alternating root depths avoids exhausting one layer and opens the subsoil.
hints: Think of the soil profile from top to bottom.

stem: In a rotation, what is a ley?

options.content: A field left bare and weed-free for one season
options.rationale: That is a bare fallow.

options.content: A legume crop grown for its grain
options.rationale: A grain legume is a crop course, not a ley.

options.content: A strip of trees planted to shelter the crops from wind
options.rationale: That is a windbreak.

options.content: Land sown to grass for a few years and grazed or cut
options.rationale: Correct.

explanation: A ley rests the soil, builds organic matter and provides grazing.

stem: Which course of a rotation should normally receive the farmyard manure?

options.content: The legume, so it fixes more nitrogen
options.rationale: Legumes need little nitrogen; manure is better used by maize.

options.content: The heavy-feeding cereal such as maize
options.rationale: Correct: it responds most to the nutrients.

options.content: The grass ley, so cattle eat the manure
options.rationale: This would waste the manure.

options.content: The bare fallow, which has no crop
options.rationale: Nutrients would be lost with nothing to use them.

explanation: Manure goes to the most demanding crop, usually maize or tobacco.
hints: Which crop needs the most nutrients?

stem: Which is a genuine limitation of crop rotation for a smallholder with 1 ha?

options.content: Rotation always reduces soil fertility
options.rationale: It usually maintains fertility.

options.content: The land must be split into small fields, some with low-value crops
options.rationale: Correct: this can reduce income.

options.content: Rotation always increases the build-up of pests and diseases in the soil
options.rationale: Rotation reduces pests.

options.content: Rotated crops can never be sold
options.rationale: Rotated crops are sold like any others.

explanation: With little land, dividing it among several crops and a ley may not give enough food or cash.

stem: A four-course rotation takes four years before each field has carried every crop once.
explanation: True. Each crop moves one field along each year.

stem: Following maize with sorghum is a good rotation because the two crops belong to different families.
explanation: False. Both are cereals of the grass family and share pests, diseases and witchweed.

stem: Match each crop with its role in a rotation.

right.content: Deep taproot that uses subsoil nutrients
Rests the soil and adds organic matter
Heavy feeder that receives the manure

explanation: Each course has a purpose in a well-designed rotation.

stem: Complete the sentence.

payload.template: Growing the same crop on the same land every year is called {{blank:a}}; each crop and its piece of land in a rotation is called a {{blank:b}}.

explanation: Monoculture; course.

stem: A farmer divides 10 ha of arable land into a four-course rotation of equal fields. Calculate the area of each course, in ha.
explanation: 10 ÷ 4 = 2.5 ha per course.

stem: Assume maize after a legume needs 30 kg/ha less nitrogen. Calculate the mass of ammonium nitrate (34.5% N) saved per hectare, in kg, to one decimal place.
explanation: 30 ÷ 0.345 = 87 kg/ha. Multiplying by 0.345 (10.4 kg) gives the nitrogen in 30 kg of fertiliser, not the fertiliser needed.
workedSolution:
1. Nitrogen saved = 30 kg/ha.
2. Ammonium nitrate = 30 ÷ (34.5 ÷ 100) = 30 ÷ 0.345.
3. = 86.96 ≈ 87 kg/ha.

stem: In a four-course rotation on 10 ha, manure is applied at 8 t/ha to the maize course only. How many tonnes of manure are needed each year?
explanation: Maize course = 10 ÷ 4 = 2.5 ha; 8 × 2.5 = 20 t. Using the whole 10 ha gives 80 t, which is wrong.
workedSolution: 1. Maize course = 10 ÷ 4 = 2.5 ha; 8 × 2.5 = 20 t. Using the whole 10 ha gives 80 t, which is wrong.

stem: Name the bacteria in legume root nodules that make legumes valuable in a rotation.
explanation: ***Rhizobium***.

stem: Explain **two** principles of crop rotation.

points.description: Alternate deep- and shallow-rooted crops.
So nutrients and water are used from different soil layers and the subsoil is opened up.
Crops of different families follow each other (or: legume before heavy feeder / include a ley).
So pests and diseases find no host and die out (or: nitrogen is supplied / soil rests and gains organic matter).

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: Deep-rooted and shallow-rooted crops are alternated, so nutrients and water are taken from different layers and the soil is not exhausted in one layer. Crops of different families follow each other, so pests and diseases that attack one family have no host and die out.

explanation: Principle plus reason.
hints: State the principle, then why it helps.

stem: Discuss **two** advantages and **two** limitations of crop rotation for a farmer near Gokwe.

points.description: Advantage: legumes add nitrogen, so less fertiliser is bought.
Advantage: pests, diseases and witchweed are reduced / several crops spread labour, income and risk.
Limitation: planning, records and knowledge of several crops are needed / land is divided into small fields.
Limitation: some courses earn less or have no reliable market / different implements and inputs are needed.

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: Rotation lets the groundnut course supply nitrogen to the next maize, cutting fertiliser costs, and it reduces witchweed and pests, while several crops spread labour and risk. However, it needs careful planning and the land is split into smaller fields, and some crops such as a ley may earn little or lack a market.

explanation: Two each side.

stem:
Sipho plans a four-course rotation on four equal fields near Chinhoyi.

| Field | Year 1 | Year 2 | Year 3 | Year 4 |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| A | Maize | Groundnuts | Cotton | Grass ley |
| B | Grass ley | Maize | Groundnuts | Cotton |
| C | Cotton | Grass ley | Maize | Groundnuts |
| D | Groundnuts | Cotton | Grass ley | ? |

parts.label: (a)
parts.stem: Which crop should replace the question mark in field D, year 4?

options.content: Groundnuts
options.rationale: Groundnuts grew in field D in year 1 and follow maize.

options.content: Maize
options.rationale: Correct: it follows the grass ley as in the other fields.

options.content: Cotton
options.rationale: Cotton grew in field D in year 2.

options.content: Grass ley
options.rationale: Field D had the ley in year 3.

parts.explanation: The order is maize, groundnuts, cotton, grass ley; after the ley comes maize.

parts.label: (b)
parts.stem: Name the crop in the plan that fixes nitrogen.

parts.label: (c)
parts.stem: Name the course that receives the manure.

parts.label: (d)
parts.stem: Explain why cotton is placed after groundnuts.

points.description: Cotton has a deep taproot whereas groundnuts are shallower, so different layers are used.
Cotton is a different family, breaking pest and disease cycles (and it uses residual nitrogen).

parts.label: (e)
parts.stem: Explain **three** benefits of including the grass ley.

points.description: Rests the soil and builds organic matter from the dense roots.
Improves soil structure and protects the soil from erosion.
Provides grazing or hay, and manure from cattle grazing it.

explanation: Complete and justify a four-course rotation.
hints: Each crop moves one field along each year.
Look for the pattern in field D.

stem:
A demonstration plot near Bindura compared continuous maize with maize grown in a rotation with a legume. Both received the same fertiliser.

| Season | Continuous maize (t/ha) | Maize in a rotation with a legume (t/ha) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | 4.6 | 4.5 |
| 2 | 4.1 | 4.7 |
| 3 | 3.7 | 4.6 |
| 4 | 3.2 | 4.8 |

parts.label: (a)
parts.stem: Calculate the percentage fall in the yield of continuous maize from season 1 to season 4, to one decimal place.

parts.label: (b)
parts.stem: Calculate the mean yield of maize in the rotation over the four seasons, in t/ha, to two decimal places.

parts.label: (c)
parts.stem: Describe the trend shown by each treatment.

points.description: Continuous maize yields fell every season.
Maize in the rotation stayed steady or rose slightly.

parts.label: (d)
parts.stem: Suggest **three** reasons for the fall in yield of continuous maize.

points.description: Build-up of maize pests and diseases (stalk borer, grey leaf spot) with a host every year.
Build-up of witchweed and other weeds adapted to maize.
Decline in soil organic matter, structure and nutrients other than those in the fertiliser.

parts.label: (e)
parts.stem: The farmer says, "The legume season earns less than maize, so rotation is not worth it." Evaluate this view.

points.description: The legume itself earns income (and food), and saves nitrogen fertiliser for the next maize.
The data show rotation keeps maize yields high, while continuous maize fell by about 30%, so long-term income is better.
Judgement: rotation is worth it over several seasons, though in one season the legume may earn less.

parts.explanation: Weigh short-term income against long-term yield.

explanation: Interpret long-term yield data and evaluate rotation.
hints: Look at the trend, not one season.

stem: Thandeka grows tobacco near Karoi and has found galls on the roots of her tobacco plants, caused by root-knot nematodes.

parts.label: (a)
parts.stem: Explain why growing tobacco on the same land every year makes the nematode problem worse.

points.description: Nematodes feed and multiply on tobacco roots every season.
So their numbers in the soil build up year after year.

parts.label: (b)
parts.stem: Suggest how a rotation could reduce the problem.

points.description: Follow tobacco with crops that are poor hosts, such as a suitable grass ley.
Without a good host for several years nematode numbers fall before tobacco is grown again.

parts.label: (c)
parts.stem: State **two** other benefits the rotation would bring to her farm.

points.description: Improved soil structure and organic matter (ley) / less erosion.
Income or grazing from other crops / spreads labour and risk.

explanation: Rotation as a control for soil pests.
hints: Nematodes need a host to survive.
